newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian forces rocket rebel hideout in Algiers.
newsitem.headline: Algerian forces rocket rebel hideout in Algiers.

text.p: Algerian security forces on Wednesday fired rockets into a central Algiers apartment block killing several suspected Moslem guerrillas after an eight-hour siege, residents said.
"The security forces completely destroyed the flat where the gunmen holed up. They hit the house with several rockets," a resident told Reuters by telephone.

Other residents said several guerrillas were killed in the attack on the 14-storey apartment block in May First square, near the spot where trade union chief Abdelhak Benhamouda was shot dead by Moslem guerrillas on January 28.
"It seems there were no survivors among the gunmen in the raided flat", said a resident, adding that the rockets hit a flat on the fifth floor of the building.
Residents said the government forces had besieged the building for more than eight hours since 2 a.m. (0100 GMT) and hundreds of people turned up to watch the drama.

"The members of the besieged group began to make their way to freedom through the wall of an adjoining house but they didn't have enough time to finish their bid," said a resident who visited the wrecked hideout.
The authorities made no comments on the sige and rocket attack.
Security forces killed leaders of Algerian Jihad Islamic Front (FIDA) last May after a two-day siege in the posh Said Hamdine neighborhood in Algiers.
FIDA, a small rebel faction based in Algiers, claimed responsibility for the assassination of Benhamouda.
Algiers has experienced several similar raids in the past three years, including a fierce gunbattle in 1994 when Algiers's district commander was shot dead in central Algiers.

Algeria's main Arab-language al Khabar newspaper said on Wednesday that troops and police on Tuesday captured bombs and destroyed guerrilla hideouts in a five-hour operation in Djebel Koukou, overlooking the Moslem fundamentalist stronghold of Bab el Oued in Algiers.
President Liamine Zeroual on Tuesday told 10 political party heads that violence was diminishing in Algeria and blamed the latest wave of killings on rival Moslem rebel groups settling scores.
"President Zeroual...appeared very optimistic about the security situation," said one of the 10 officials, speaking to Reuters by telephone from Algiers.
The meeting had been called to discuss preparations for parliamentary elections planned for May 29 or June 5.

More than 300 people have died in the past four weeks -- coinciding with the Moslem fast of Ramadan -- in massacres and bomb attacks in Algiers and neighbouring hamlets and towns. The authorities have blamed Moslem rebels for the deaths.
